query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a nominally single‐phase high-entropy alloy (HEA), the emergence of brittleness under service conditions is primarily driven by deformation-induced local compositional segregation that leads to intragranular nano-phase separation. This process creates nanoscale regions with distinct stacking fault energies and incompatible deformation mechanisms, which act as internal crack initiation sites—an effect analogous to grain-boundary embrittlement in conventional alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single-phase high-entropy alloy with a complex multi-element composition before any severe mechanical or thermal loading.
generation.intervention: Subject the HEA to controlled thermomechanical treatments (e.g., high-strain deformation combined with moderate thermal annealing) designed to trigger local compositional fluctuations without triggering bulk intermetallic precipitation at grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: Service conditions involving high mechanical strain and/or elevated temperatures that favor enhanced atomic mobility and local elemental redistribution, within the operating load and temperature ranges typical for demanding engineering applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale, intragranular regions of compositional inhomogeneity (e.g., Cu-rich versus Cu-depleted areas) with associated variations in stacking fault energy and dislocation mobility.
generation.mechanism: Under applied load and heat, atomic diffusion along dislocation lines and stacking faults promotes local phase separation within grains. These nanoscale segregated regions exhibit different mechanical responses (e.g., one region accommodating deformation via twinning and the other via dislocation glide), leading to internal stress concentrations and reduced plastic compatibility, which in turn reduce toughness by promoting premature microcrack nucleation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the initial homogeneous state, the treated HEA will display a measurable decrease in toughness and ductility. High-resolution microscopy should reveal nanoscale compositional segregates intragranularly, and mechanical testing should show lower fracture toughness than samples where such segregation is suppressed. Unlike conventional alloys where embrittlement is primarily associated with grain-boundary segregates or precipitates, these changes will occur within grains.
generation.baseline: The initial single-phase, compositionally uniform HEA exhibiting high toughness and ductility before undergoing any significant deformation or thermal exposure.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be significant under conditions of severe plastic deformation and moderate annealing temperatures that allow for local diffusion, but not high enough to activate extensive grain-boundary precipitation or coarsening. Under very low-strain or room-temperature conditions, the HEA should largely retain its original toughness.
generation.uncertainty: While the hypothesis is supported by observed nano-phase separation phenomena in some HEA systems, the precise threshold for the onset of deleterious segregation, the interplay of different elements in complex compositions, and the quantitative effects on toughness need further experimental clarification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples from the same initial single-phase material. Subject one set to the controlled thermomechanical treatment expected to induce intragranular nano-phase separation, while keeping the other set as a control (minimal strain and lower thermal exposure). Perform high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HR-TEM) to assess the presence, size, and distribution of nanoscale compositional segregates in the grains. Then, conduct fracture toughness tests (e.g., via standardized KJ_IC measurements) on both sets.
measurements: HR-TEM imaging for detection of intragranular nano-phase segregates
Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) mapping for compositional fluctuations
Fracture toughness (KJ_IC) and ductility measurements from mechanical testing
Comparison of dislocation behavior and evidence of twinning via in situ straining experiments
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If treated samples do not exhibit significant intragranular compositional segregation and there is no corresponding decrease in fracture toughness compared to the control, then the hypothesis that local nano-phase separation is responsible for brittleness in the HEA will be falsified.

Role of Cu in Nanostructural Relationship Between Phase Separation and Deformation-Induced Twinning in Heavily Drawn Non-Equiatomic High-Entropy Alloy Wire

Abstract: This study investigates the influence of Cu addition on the nanostructural evolution and mechanical performance of a heavily drawn non-equiatomic CoCu1.71FeMnNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) wire. Through systematic microstructural and compositional analysis, we examine how Cu constituent affects phase separation behavior and promotes deformation-induced nano-twinning in another phase counterpart. The designed HEA wire exhibits an elongated ultrafine dual face-centered cubic (fcc) lamella structure (i.e., Co-Fe-rich and Cu-rich phases) that emerges through compositional segregation by spontaneous phase separation from the as-cast state. High-resolution electron microscopy reveals the dislocation wall boundaries stabilized by nanoscale phase interfaces. The cold-drawn CoCu1.71FeMnNi wire features an impressive combination of strength and ductility, as well as an ultimate tensile strength of nearly ~2 GPa with an elongation of over ~6%. Nanoscale origins of the damage tolerance of the high-entropy alloy CrMnFeCoNi

Abstract: AbstractDamage tolerance can be an elusive characteristic of structural materials requiring both high strength and ductility, properties that are often mutually exclusive. High-entropy alloys are of interest in this regard. Specifically, the single-phase CrMnFeCoNi alloy displays tensile strength levels of ∼1 GPa, excellent ductility (∼60–70%) and exceptional fracture toughness (KJIc>200 MPa√m). Here through the use of in situ straining in an aberration-corrected transmission electron microscope, we report on the salient atomistic to micro-scale mechanisms underlying the origin of these properties. We identify a synergy of multiple deformation mechanisms, rarely achieved in metallic alloys, which generates high strength, work hardening and ductility, including the easy motion of Shockley partials, their interactions to form stacking-fault parallelepipeds, and arrest at planar slip bands of undissociated dislocations. Exceptional damage-tolerance of a medium-entropy alloy CrCoNi at cryogenic temperatures

Abstract: High-entropy alloys are an intriguing new class of metallic materials that derive their properties from being multi-element systems that can crystallize as a single phase, despite containing high concentrations of five or more elements with different crystal structures. Here we examine an equiatomic medium-entropy alloy containing only three elements, CrCoNi, as a single-phase face-centred cubic solid solution, which displays strength-toughness properties that exceed those of all high-entropy alloys and most multi-phase alloys. At room temperature, the alloy shows tensile strengths of almost 1 GPa, failure strains of ∼70% and KJIc fracture-toughness values above 200 MPa m1/2; at cryogenic temperatures strength, ductility and toughness of the CrCoNi alloy improve to strength levels above 1.3 GPa, failure strains up to 90% and KJIc values of 275 MPa m1/2. Such properties appear to result from continuous steady strain hardening, which acts to suppress plastic instability, resulting from pronounced dislocation activity and deformation-induced nano-twinning.
